lessonTitle: Solar Radiation Basics: Incidence Angle, Absorbed Radiation and Selective Surfaces

blocks.text: On a clear December noon in Madrid a flat-plate collector lying flat on the roof receives less than half the energy of an identical one tilted to face the low southern sun, though both see the same sky. How much of the sun's beam a surface intercepts depends on the angle between the rays and the surface normal, and how much of that energy it keeps depends on the coating.

blocks.markdown: The sun's direct (beam) radiation is described by the irradiance $G_{b,n}$ (W/m$^2$) measured on a surface held normal to the rays. A collector surface at some other orientation intercepts only the component along its own normal. The **angle of incidence** $\theta$ is the angle between the incoming beam and the normal to the collector surface, so the beam irradiance on the surface is $G_b=G_{b,n}\cos\theta$.

blocks.title: Angle of incidence
blocks.text: The angle of incidence $\theta$ is the angle between the sun's rays and the normal to a surface; $\theta=0$ means the sun is directly overhead of the surface and $\cos\theta=1$. When $\cos\theta\le0$ the sun is behind the surface and no beam radiation is received.

blocks.markdown: Five angles locate the surface relative to the sun: the latitude $\phi$ of the site, the declination $\delta$ (the sun's angle north of the equatorial plane, between $-23.45^\circ$ and $+23.45^\circ$), the hour angle $\omega$ (15$^\circ$ per hour, zero at solar noon, positive in the afternoon), the surface tilt $\beta$ from horizontal and the surface azimuth $\gamma$ (zero for a surface facing the equator). The general relation is long, but for a surface facing due south in the northern hemisphere ($\gamma=0$) it simplifies.

blocks.caption: Equator-facing surface ($\gamma=0$) at latitude $\phi$, tilt $\beta$, declination $\delta$, hour angle $\omega$

blocks.title: Angle of incidence and absorbed power
blocks.prompt: A south-facing collector (area 2.0 m$^2$, absorptance 0.95) is tilted at $\beta=45^\circ$ at latitude $\phi=35^\circ$ N. At $\delta=20^\circ$ and $\omega=30^\circ$ (two hours after solar noon) the beam normal irradiance is 800 W/m$^2$. Find $\theta$ and the absorbed beam power.

steps.text: Absorbed power is absorptance times irradiance on the surface times area.

blocks.answer: The sun is 42.1 degrees off the normal, so the surface gets 594 W/m$^2$ of beam radiation and absorbs 1128 W (ignoring diffuse and reflected components).

blocks.title: Absorptance is the fraction kept
blocks.text: For an opaque surface, $\alpha+\rho=1$, where $\alpha$ is the fraction of incident solar radiation absorbed and $\rho$ the fraction reflected. A surface with $\alpha=0.95$ keeps 95 % of what reaches it. The absorbed power is $Q_{abs}=\alpha G A$, with $G$ the irradiance on the surface (W/m$^2$) and $A$ the area (m$^2$). Real coatings lose a few percent more at large $\theta$.

blocks.markdown: A hot absorber also loses heat. Besides convection and conduction, it radiates to the cold sky at an effective temperature $T_{sky}$. The radiation loss is $q_{rad}=\varepsilon\sigma(T_p^4-T_{sky}^4)$, with $\varepsilon$ the emittance of the surface, $\sigma=5.67\times10^{-8}$ W/m$^2$K$^4$ and temperatures in kelvin. A black paint has $\alpha\approx\varepsilon\approx0.95$, so it loses heat as well as it gains it. The remedy is a **selective surface**.

blocks.title: Selective surface
blocks.text: A selective surface has high absorptance in the solar wavelength band (about 0.3 to 2.5 $\mu$m) and low emittance in the infrared band where a collector at 50 to 150 $^\circ$C emits (about 3 to 30 $\mu$m). Because the two bands barely overlap, a coating can be both a strong absorber and a poor emitter.

blocks.caption: Typical values, which vary with manufacturer and temperature.

blocks.title: Radiative loss with and without a selective coating
blocks.prompt: An absorber plate is at 80 $^\circ$C (353.15 K) facing a sky at 15 $^\circ$C (288.15 K). Compare the radiative loss per square metre for black paint ($\varepsilon=0.95$) and a selective surface ($\varepsilon=0.10$).
blocks.answer: The selective surface cuts radiative loss from about 466 to 49 W/m$^2$, a factor of 9.5, while keeping nearly the same $\alpha$.

items: The beam irradiance on a tilted surface is the normal irradiance times $\cos\theta$; diffuse sky and ground-reflected components must be added in practice.
At solar noon on a day with declination $\delta$, a south-facing surface at latitude $\phi$ with tilt $\beta$ has $\theta=|\phi-\beta-\delta|$.
Absorptance and emittance depend on wavelength and on temperature; selective surfaces exploit the difference between solar and infrared bands.
A fixed tilt close to latitude maximises annual collection; a steeper tilt favours winter.

blocks.title: Check your calculator mode
blocks.text: Always check whether your calculator is in degrees or radians. A common error is the sign of $\phi-\beta$ when the tilt exceeds latitude. If $\cos\theta<0$, the sun is behind the surface and the beam contribution is zero, not negative.

points: The angle of incidence $\theta$ sets the beam irradiance on a surface, $G_b=G_{b,n}\cos\theta$.
Absorbed solar power is $Q_{abs}=\alpha GA$, with $\alpha$ the absorptance of the surface and $G$ the irradiance on it.
Radiative loss is $\varepsilon\sigma(T_p^4-T_{sky}^4)$ and grows as the fourth power of absolute temperature.
A selective surface combines high solar absorptance with low infrared emittance, greatly reducing radiative loss at operating temperature.

questions.stem: A collector faces due south at latitude 50 degrees N and is tilted 30 degrees from horizontal. At a declination of 15 degrees and an hour angle of -45 degrees (three hours before solar noon, morning), find the angle of incidence in degrees. Use cos(theta) = sin(delta) sin(phi - beta) + cos(delta) cos(phi - beta) cos(omega).
questions.explanation: With phi - beta = 20 degrees, sin(15)sin(20) = 0.0885 and cos(15)cos(20)cos(-45) = 0.6419, so cos(theta) = 0.7303 and theta = 43.1 degrees. The cosine is even in the hour angle, so the sign of omega does not matter.

questions.stem: On the winter solstice (declination -23.45 degrees) at solar noon, a south-facing collector at latitude 25 degrees N is tilted at 25 degrees from horizontal. What is the angle of incidence?

options.text: 23.45 degrees, because $\theta=|\phi-\beta-\delta|$ at noon
0 degrees, because tilt equals latitude
48.45 degrees, because the declination adds to the latitude
25 degrees, because the angle of incidence equals the tilt

distractorRationale.b: Tilt equal to latitude gives normal incidence only at the equinoxes, when the declination is zero.
distractorRationale.c: That would be $|\phi-\beta+\delta|$ with the sign of $\delta$ reversed.
distractorRationale.d: The tilt alone does not determine $\theta$; the sun's declination also matters.

questions.explanation: At solar noon $\cos\theta=\cos(\phi-\beta-\delta)$ for an equator-facing surface, so $\theta=|25-25-(-23.45)|=23.45^\circ$. In winter the sun is lower than at the equinox, so a collector tilted at latitude is slightly too flat.

questions.stem: The solar irradiance on the plane of a collector is 650 W/m^2. The absorber has an absorptance of 0.92 and the collector area is 3.2 m^2. Calculate the absorbed solar power in W.
questions.explanation: Absorbed power is alpha x G x A = 0.92 x 650 x 3.2 = 1914 W. The remaining 8 percent of the incident energy is reflected, so absorbed plus reflected equals the 2080 W that reaches the surface.

questions.stem: The beam normal irradiance is 900 W/m$^2$, the angle of incidence is 40 degrees and a 1.5 m$^2$ absorber has absorptance 0.90. What beam power is absorbed?

options.text: About 1215 W
About 931 W
About 781 W
About 1034 W

distractorRationale.a: This ignores the cosine factor and treats the beam as normal to the surface.
distractorRationale.c: This uses the sine of the angle of incidence instead of the cosine.
distractorRationale.d: This forgets the absorptance, so it is the power incident, not absorbed.

questions.explanation: The irradiance on the surface is $900\cos40^\circ=689$ W/m$^2$. Multiplying by area 1.5 m$^2$ and absorptance 0.90 gives 931 W. The cosine reduces the intercepted beam and the absorptance reduces what is kept.

questions.stem: An absorber plate at 90 degrees Celsius (363.15 K) faces a sky at an effective temperature of 5 degrees Celsius (278.15 K). It carries a selective coating with infrared emittance 0.12. Take sigma = 5.67 x 10^-8 W/m^2 K^4 and find the radiative heat loss per unit area in W/m^2.
questions.explanation: The fourth-power difference is 363.15^4 - 278.15^4 = 1.1406 x 10^10 K^4, and sigma times this is about 647 W/m^2 for a black body. With emittance 0.12 the loss is 77.6 W/m^2. A surface with emittance 0.90 would lose 7.5 times as much.

questions.stem: Which description fits an ideal selective surface for a solar absorber at 100 degrees Celsius?

options.text: High absorptance at wavelengths below about 2.5 micrometres and low emittance at longer infrared wavelengths
Low absorptance at solar wavelengths and high emittance at infrared wavelengths
High absorptance and high emittance at all wavelengths
Low absorptance and low emittance at all wavelengths

questions.correctOptionText: High absorptance at wavelengths below about 2.5 micrometres and low emittance at longer infrared wavelengths

distractorRationale.b: This would reject sunlight and radiate heat away: the opposite of what a collector needs.
distractorRationale.c: This is flat black paint; it absorbs well but also loses heat by radiation.
distractorRationale.d: This is a polished metal mirror, a poor absorber that also has low radiative loss.

questions.explanation: Solar radiation comes from a 5800 K source and sits mostly below 2.5 $\mu$m, whereas an absorber at 100 degrees Celsius emits at 3 to 30 $\mu$m. A coating that absorbs strongly in the first band and emits weakly in the second keeps heat gained and loses little.

questions.stem: An opaque collector surface has solar absorptance 0.93. What fraction of the incident solar radiation is reflected?

options.text: 7 %, because for an opaque surface the absorptance and reflectance sum to one
93 %, because absorptance is the same as reflectance
0 %, because collector surfaces are black
14 %, because radiation is reflected twice before it is absorbed

questions.correctOptionText: 7 %, because for an opaque surface the absorptance and reflectance sum to one

distractorRationale.c: A real surface still reflects a few percent.
distractorRationale.d: There is no such doubling; the fractions sum to one.

questions.explanation: Energy conservation for an opaque surface gives $\alpha+\rho=1$, so $\rho=0.07$. That small reflected portion still represents a loss that glazing and coatings aim to reduce.

questions.stem: Explain what the angle of incidence is and why a collector fixed at a tilt near the site latitude is a good compromise for annual energy collection, but is not optimal on every day of the year.
markingGuide: Defines $\theta$ as the angle between the sun's rays and the surface normal and states $G_b=G_{b,n}\cos\theta$
Explains that the sun's noon altitude changes with declination between $\pm23.45^\circ$ over the year
Tilt equal to latitude gives $\theta=|\delta|$ at noon, so it is normal at equinox and within 23.45 degrees at the solstices
States that in winter a steeper tilt would reduce $\theta$ (and in summer a flatter one would)
Mentions that hour angle also changes $\theta$ through the day, so the fixed surface sees $\cos\theta$ reduced in the morning and evening
questions.explanation: The cosine of the angle of incidence determines how much beam radiation a fixed surface intercepts. Since the sun's noon position moves seasonally, any fixed tilt is a compromise, and a tilt near latitude centres the error evenly through the year.

questions.stem: A flat plate collector operates with the absorber at 90 degrees Celsius. Explain, with reference to radiation properties, why replacing black paint with a selective surface improves the useful heat output, and why this gain is larger at high operating temperatures than at low ones.
markingGuide: Radiative loss is $\varepsilon\sigma(T_p^4-T_{sky}^4)$ so a smaller $\varepsilon$ reduces loss in proportion
Selective surface keeps $\alpha$ near 0.95 while $\varepsilon$ falls from about 0.95 to about 0.1
Absorbed solar energy is nearly unchanged but losses are much smaller, so useful heat rises
Loss depends on the fourth power of absolute temperature, so the radiative term grows rapidly as $T_p$ increases
So the saving is larger at high temperature; at low temperature (pool heating) convective loss dominates and selectivity matters little
questions.explanation: The useful output is the absorbed solar energy minus losses. A selective coating reduces the radiative loss while preserving absorption, and because radiation grows as $T^4$, the benefit is greatest in hotter collectors.

questions.stem: For a given surface and time, the angle-of-incidence formula gives cos(theta) = -0.20. The beam normal irradiance is 700 W/m^2. What beam irradiance does the surface receive?

options.text: -140 W/m^2, which subtracts from the diffuse radiation
140 W/m^2, taking the magnitude of the cosine
Zero, because the sun is behind the surface and it receives no direct beam
700 W/m^2, because the beam normal irradiance is unaffected by orientation

questions.correctOptionText: Zero, because the sun is behind the surface and it receives no direct beam

distractorRationale.a: Beam radiation cannot be negative; the surface just receives none.
distractorRationale.b: The beam strikes the back of the surface, which is not the absorbing side.
distractorRationale.d: The beam normal value is measured perpendicular to the rays; a surface only intercepts the component along its normal.

questions.explanation: A negative cosine means the angle of incidence exceeds 90 degrees and the sun is behind the surface plane. The beam contribution is then set to zero, and only diffuse and reflected radiation can reach the surface.
